---
title: "Publishing a record"
description: |
  Use the `publish` command to create a new deposit and publish it as a record.
order: 1
---

The main purpose of zen-do is to simplify the process of publishing records on
Zenodo. This page walks you through how to use zen-do to create and publish a
record on Zenodo.

{{< include /docs/includes/_deposit-vs-record.qmd >}}

## Creating and filling in `.zenodo.toml`

In order to publish on Zenodo, you need to create and fill out the metadata for
your (future) published record in the `.zenodo.toml` file (or a similarly named
TOML file). You can create an empty one with the `zen-do init` command.

{{< include /docs/includes/_use-uv.qmd >}}

The file or files that will be part of the published record must be in the same
folder as the `.zenodo.toml` file or in a subfolder within that folder (see our
[design docs](/docs/design/interface/inputs.qmd) for more details about this).
This allows you to organise your files in different ways depending on what you
want to publish. For example, you could have one Zenodo deposit for a Git
repository or one deposit for a [Quarto](https://quarto.org) output file in a
folder.

However, a single folder could contain multiple deposits. For example, one
deposit could contain the source files for creating a Quarto book (such as the
entire Git repository) and one deposit could be the generated PDF book. In this
case, there would be two `.zenodo.toml` files in the same folder, but with
different prefixes (e.g. `.zenodo.toml` for the Git repository and
`.pdf.zenodo.toml` for the PDF).

For now, we'll keep it simple. We want to create a Zenodo deposit and eventual
record for a PDF output of a scientific analysis done in a Quarto document. In
this guide, the PDF file will be called `analysis-report.pdf`.

We start with creating an empty `.zenodo.toml` file in the folder that has the
Quarto document (note that they must be in the same folder).

<!-- TODO: Convert into an executable code chunk -->

```bash {filename="Terminal"}
zen-do init
```

This creates an empty `.zenodo.toml` file. If you open it, you should see
something like below:

```toml {filename=".zenodo.toml"}
title = ""
upload_type = ""
zendo_id = "<github-username>:<repo-name>:<output-type>"

[[creators]]
name = ""
affiliation = ""
orcid = ""

[[related_identifiers]]
identifier = ""
relation = ""
resource_type = ""
scheme = ""
```

Notice the `zendo_id` field in the newly created `.zenodo.toml` file. zen-do
needs this field to keep track of projects. It is needed for all tasks,
such as creating a new deposit or updating an existing
one and publishing a record from the changes. The `zendo_id` key needs to
be a value that is unique to the (future) deposit of all the deposits in your
Zenodo account. As long as you use the pattern shown above
(`"<github-username>:<repo-name>:<output-type>"`), it should be unique enough.
We assume (and strongly recommend) you store your project as a Git repository
and that you save it on GitHub, so you can use your username or organization
name along with the repository name as the base of this `zendo_id`. Since in
this guide we want to publish a report, we can use that as the `<output-type>`
as `report`.

::: callout-tip
If you don't use GitHub, follow the naming scheme
`your-name:project-name:output-type`. This helps to ensure that the URN will be
(very likely) unique to your deposit and allow zen-do to identify if any deposit
with that identifier already exists on your Zenodo account.
:::

In our case, we can update the value with:

```toml {filename=".zenodo.toml"}
...
zendo_id = "seedcase-project:zen-do:report-pdf"
...
```

Once you've filled it in, you can fill in the other values in the `.zenodo.toml`
file. After you've filled in the `.zenodo.toml` file, it's time to create a
deposit!

## Creating a (draft) deposit

You eventually want to make a published record based on your newly created
`.zenodo.toml` file. But you don't yet have a deposit. A record can only be
created from a deposit. If a `.zenodo.toml` file doesn't have an associated
deposit on your Zenodo account, using `zen-do publish` will create that deposit
for you. If you want to check whether a deposit already exists, you can use
`zen-do get`:

```bash {filename="Terminal"}
zen-do get
```

This command will read your `.zenodo.toml` file and check your Zenodo account
for any deposit that has the value `zendo_id` in it. If it finds something, it
will print the deposit details to your terminal, otherwise, it will let you know
it hasn't found anything.

By default, running `zen-do publish` will create a new deposit and immediately
publish a new record from that deposit, though it will prompt you to confirm.
When creating deposits for the first time, it's good practice to use the [Zenodo
sandbox](https://sandbox.zenodo.org/) and make a draft first. Then to check the
metadata in the newly created draft deposit to confirm. If it looks as you
expect (the information is there that you want there), you can then try creating
a record in the sandbox. So, let's try making a draft in Zenodo's sandbox.
zen-do's `publish` command needs the file to upload along with the
`.zenodo.toml` file, which it looks for in the current directory by default.
Using `publish` will always prompt you to confirm your actions, as some actions
are irreversible (see note below).

```bash {filename="Terminal"}
zen-do publish --file analysis-report.pdf --sandbox --draft
```

::: callout-tip
If you wanted to add multiple files, you can use `--file` multiple times:

```bash {filename="Terminal"}
zen-do publish \
  --file analysis-report.pdf \
  --file supplemental-details.pdf \
  --sandbox --draft
```
:::

Next, open up the [Zenodo sandbox website](https://sandbox.zenodo.org/), go to your "dashboard", and open the newly
created draft deposit. Does the content of the page match what is in your
`.zenodo.toml` file? Great!

Because you made a draft, you could either manually click "publish" or you could
try it with zen-do. Let's try publishing with zen-do! Because you created a
draft you need to discard it first. That's what the `discard` command is for:

```bash {filename="Terminal"}
zen-do discard --sandbox
```

You can try re-running the command to publish as a record in the sandbox:

```bash {filename="Terminal"}
zen-do publish --file analysis-report.pdf --sandbox
```

Now when you go to your Zenodo sandbox account, you should see a new record for
the deposit.

## Publishing your first record

If you're satisfied with how `publish` works with `--sandbox`, it's time to
officially publish the report on Zenodo! It's as easy as removing the
`--sandbox` argument.

::: callout-important
Be **very** careful and certain about what you officially publish on Zenodo (not
the sandbox). Once something has been published and a record with a DOI has been
created, it **cannot** be deleted fully!
:::

```bash {filename="Terminal"}
zen-do publish --file analysis-report.pdf
```

This command prompts you to confirm. Saying yes will now create an official
record and associated DOI for your analysis! You can check it from your terminal
by using `get`:

```bash {filename="Terminal"}
zen-do get
```

::: callout-tip
If you want to include zen-do in a GitHub workflow or some continuous delivery
process, you can use the `--yes` argument to bypass the prompt. But be very
careful with this.

```bash {filename="Terminal"}
zen-do publish --file analysis-report.pdf --yes
```
:::

## Publishing another record

For some outputs, like a scientific paper, you may only ever need to create one
record. However, for some types of output, especially ones with versions or with
frequent changes, such as a book or course material, you'll probably want to
create a new record for those new changes to the file or files. Publishing a new
record of an existing deposit is as easy as using the same command as above!

```bash {filename="Terminal"}
zen-do publish --file analysis-report.pdf
```

::: callout-important
To update a deposit with a new file and create a new record including that file,
zen-do **requires** the `zendo_id` value in the `.zenodo.toml` file. This ID
ensures that a new record is correctly created in the existing deposit on your
account.
:::

::: callout-tip
If you only want to update the metadata, *but not change the file*, use the
`zen-do update` command. This command doesn't create a new record and only edits
the metadata of an existing deposit or record.
:::
